claim: The side chain of H3 T118 is close enough to form a hydrogen bond with the DNA.
source: The side chain of H3 T118 (red) is close enough to form a hydrogen bond with the DNA (grey).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the structural position of H3 T118 relative to DNA in the nucleosome structure.

claim: The H3 T118ph antibody is highly specific in dot-blot assays.
source: The antisera were highly specific in dot-blot assays (Figure 1B)
evidence: Dot-blot assay data shown in Figure 1B demonstrates antibody specificity.

claim: The H3 T118ph antibody recognizes a single protein identical in size to histone H3 in western blot analysis of total protein extracts from HeLa cells.
source: The antisera were highly specific in dot-blot assays (Figure 1B) and recognize a single protein identical in size to histone H3 in western blot analysis of total protein extracts from HeLa cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1C shows a single band at the expected size for histone H3.

claim: Treatment with the protein phosphatase 1 and 2A inhibitor calyculin A increases H3 T118ph signal.
source: This signal in western blots was increased by treating the cells with the protein phosphatase 1 and 2A inhibitor calyculin A for 3 hr, indicating that the H3 T118ph antibody recognized phosphorylated H3 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1D shows increased signal upon calyculin A treatment.

claim: H3 T118ph levels dramatically increase as cells enter mitosis.
source: In concordance with previously published mass spectrometry results (Olsen et al., 2010), we observed a dramatic increase in H3 T118ph levels as cells entered mitosis (Figure 1E).
evidence: Western blot time course data in Figure 1E and citation to mass spectrometry results.

claim: The H3 T118ph antibody immunoprecipitates H3 from cells released into mitosis.
source: The antibody also recognized H3 T118ph in its native conformation, because it immunoprecipitated H3 from cells released into mitosis (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: H3 T118ph is restricted to mitotic cells during prophase through anaphase and is greatly diminished in interphase.
source: Using immunofluorescence analysis, we found that H3 T118ph was restricted to mitotic cells during prophase through anaphase and was greatly diminished in interphase (Figure 1G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 1G showing cell cycle-specific localization.

claim: H3 T118ph signal is detected as discrete foci on chromatin only in prophase and pro-metaphase.
source: Specifically, H3 T118ph signal was detected as discrete foci on chromatin only in prophase and pro-metaphase.
evidence: Immunofluorescence observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: H3 T118ph co-localizes with centrosomes through all phases of mitosis.
source: Additionally, H3 T118ph co-localized with centrosomes through all phases of mitosis (Figure 1G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 1G showing co-localization with α-tubulin.

claim: Non-chromatin bound histones localize to the centrosomes for proteasome-mediated degradation during mitosis.
source: This is a consequence of non-chromatin bound histones localizing to the centrosomes for proteasome-mediated degradation during mitosis (C. Wike and J.K. Tyler, manuscript submitted).
evidence: Citation to unpublished manuscript.

claim: During anaphase, the H3 T118ph antibodies detect the spindle mid-body.
source: During anaphase, the H3 T118ph antibodies also detected the spindle mid-body (Figure 1G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 1G.

claim: The localization pattern of H3 T118ph is similar in HeLa, HMEC, WI-38 and MCF10A cells.
source: The localization pattern of H3 T118ph was not unique to HeLa cells, nor cancer cell lines, because it was similar in HMEC, WI-38 and MCF10A cells (data not shown).
evidence: Statement of observation across multiple cell lines.

claim: The H3 T118ph signal is specifically competed away by an H3 T118ph peptide.
source: Finally, the H3 T118ph signal was specifically competed away by an H3 T118ph peptide (Figure 1H).
evidence: Peptide competition assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Threonine 118 and the surrounding residues are highly conserved among metazoan H3 proteins.
source: Threonine 118 and the surrounding residues are highly conserved among metazoan H3 proteins.
evidence: Statement based on sequence analysis.

claim: In D. melanogaster S2 cells, H3 T118ph localizes to chromatin and centrosomes during mitosis.
source: In D. melanogaster S2 cells, H3 T118ph localized to chromatin and centrosomes during mitosis (data not shown).
evidence: Statement of observation in Drosophila cells.

claim: During pro-metaphase in C. elegans, H3 T118ph localizes along the outside edges of chromosomes, indicative of centromeric localization on holocentric chromosomes.
source: During pro-metaphase, H3 T118ph was localized along the outside edges of chromosomes, indicative of centromeric localization on holocentric chromosomes in C. elegans (Figure 2A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in C. elegans shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon CENP-A knockdown in C. elegans, H3 T118ph is diminished from the chromatin.
source: To determine if the localization of H3 T118ph along the arms of chromosomes was dependent on the centromeric chromatin structure, we used siRNA to the centromeric histone variant CENP-A to abolish the centromeres. Upon CENP-A knockdown, H3 T118ph is diminished from the chromatin (Figure 2A).
evidence: RNAi experiment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mitotic enrichment of H3 T118ph is conserved amongst metazoans.
source: These data demonstrate that mitotic enrichment of H3 T118ph is conserved amongst metazoans.
evidence: Observations across multiple metazoan species (C. elegans, Drosophila, human).

claim: H3 T118ph localizes to centromeres and its localization is dependent on intact centromeres.
source: Furthermore, H3 T118ph localizes to centromeres and its localization is dependent on intact centromeres.
evidence: CENP-A knockdown experiment in C. elegans shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H3 T118ph co-localizes with CENP-A in human cells in prophase and pro-metaphase.
source: Indeed, we found that H3 T118ph co-localized with CENP-A in human cells in prophase and pro-metaphase (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence co-localization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The prophase to metaphase timing of the appearance and disappearance of H3 T118ph on centromeres is distinct from other mitotic H3 phosphorylation events.
source: Noteworthy, the prophase to metaphase timing of the appearance and disappearance of H3 T118ph on centromeres is distinct from other mitotic H3 phosphorylation events. For example, H3 S10ph (Crosio et al., 2002) and H3 T3ph (Polioudaki et al., 2004) remain on chromosome arms and centromeres, respectively, through anaphase. CENP-A S7ph (Zeitlin et al., 2001) remains through metaphase, while H3 T118ph is lost from centromeres in metaphase coincident with chromosome alignment.
evidence: Comparison with published timing of other histone phosphorylation marks and observations from Figure 2B.

claim: H3 T118ph foci do not always perfectly colocalize with CENP-A, but sometimes appear adjacent to CENP-A foci.
source: H3 T118ph foci did not always perfectly colocalize with CENP-A, but sometimes appeared to be adjacent to CENP-A foci.
evidence: Immunofluorescence observations described in text.

claim: In mitotic spreads treated with colcemid, H3 T118ph localizes to the inner centromere while CENP-A remains on the outer-centromere.
source: Indeed, detailed inspection of mitotic spreads revealed that H3 T118ph localized to the inner centromere when cells were treated with the microtubule destabilizing drug colcemid while CENP-A remained on the outer-centromere (Figure 2C).
evidence: Mitotic spread data with colcemid treatment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The distinct localization of CENP-A and H3 T118ph emphasizes that the H3 T118ph signal is not due to phosphorylation of CENP-A per se.
source: The distinct localization of CENP-A and H3 T118ph emphasizes that the H3 T118ph signal is not due to phosphorylation of CENP-A per se.
evidence: Inference from distinct localization patterns observed in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon colcemid treatment, the interkinetochore distance is decreased.
source: Importantly, upon colcemid treatment, where microtubule attachment is lost, the interkinetochore distance is decreased (Uchida et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to published work on colcemid effects.

claim: When there is dynamic microtubule attachment promoting tension and kinetochore stretching, H3 T118ph exists in two foci per chromosome that correlate with, but are larger than, the two CENP-A foci, consistent with pericentromeric localization.
source: Therefore we asked when there is dynamic microtubule attachment, promoting tension and kinetochore stretching, what is the true H3 T118ph signal at the centromere. H3 T118ph existed in two foci per chromosome that correlate well with, but are larger than, the two CENP-A foci (Figure 2D) consistent with pericentromeric localization.
evidence: Mitotic spread data without colcemid shown in Figure 2D.

claim: H3 T118ph appears to occur along the chromosome arms in mitotic spreads.
source: We noted that H3 T118ph also appears to occur along the chromosome arms in mitotic spreads (Figure 2D).
evidence: Observation from mitotic spread data in Figure 2D.

claim: H3 T118ph is detectable at the centromere partially overlapping with CENP-A and at weaker foci at discrete intervals along the chromosome arms on extended chromatin fibers.
source: Indeed, H3 T118ph was detectable at the centromere partially overlapping with CENP-A and at weaker foci at discrete intervals along the chromosome arms on extended chromatin fibers (Figure 2E).
evidence: Extended chromatin fiber data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Aurora-A was the only cell cycle regulated kinase able to efficiently phosphorylate H3 T118 from among the three positive kinases in the ProQinase kinase screen.
source: We utilized a ProQinase kinase screen to test 190 recombinant kinases for their ability to phosphorylate H3 T118 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Aurora-A was the only cell cycle regulated kinase able to efficiently phosphorylate H3 T118 from among the three positive kinases, arbitrarily defined as having an activity above 3000 cpm.
evidence: Kinase screen data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aurora-B and Aurora-C do not phosphorylate H3 T118.
source: Absence of phosphorylation of H3 T118 by Aurora-B and Aurora-C further validated Aurora-A as the kinase of H3 T118 (Figure 3A).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Aurora-B INCENP could not phosphorylate the T118 peptide.
source: We independently confirmed that Aurora-B INCENP could not phosphorylate the T118 peptide, including an H3 S10 peptide as a positive control (data not shown).
evidence: Statement of experimental result.

claim: Two different inhibitors to Aurora-A eradicate the H3 T118ph signal.
source: Two different inhibitors to Aurora-A eradicated the H3 T118ph signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data with Aurora-A inhibitors shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Upon Aurora-A knockdown, H3 T118ph is undetectable on chromatin.
source: Upon Aurora-A knockdown, which eradicated most of the Aurora-A protein and activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), H3 T118ph was undetectable on chromatin (Figure 3B).
evidence: siRNA knockdown and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3B and 3—figure supplement 2B, 3A.

claim: Knockdown of TPX2, a known activator of Aurora-A, greatly reduces H3 T118ph.
source: In agreement with Aurora-A being the bona fide H3 T118 kinase, knockdown of TPX2, a known activator of Aurora-A (Kufer et al., 2002), greatly reduced H3 T118ph (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: shRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C and citation to TPX2 function.

claim: Aurora-A mediates H3 T118 phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Aurora-A mediates H3 T118 phosphorylation.
evidence: Integration of multiple experimental results (kinase screen, inhibitors, knockdown).

claim: Transient transfection of HEK 293TR cells with plasmids expressing histone H3:YFP where T118 was mutated to E or I leads to a significantly increased incidence of lagging chromosomes.
source: Transient transfection of HEK 293TR cells with plasmids expressing histone H3:YFP where T118 was mutated to E or I led to a significantly increased incidence of lagging chromosomes (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Cells expressing H3 T118E:YFP or H3 T118I:YFP have significant delays in cytokinesis.
source: Using time-lapse microscopy, we found that cells expressing H3 T118E:YFP or H3 T118I:YFP had significant delays in cytokinesis (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Whenever a lagging chromosome is evident, there is an accompanying delay in the subsequent cytokinesis, regardless of the transfected construct.
source: Furthermore, whenever a lagging chromosome was evident, there also was an accompanying delay in the subsequent cytokinesis, regardless of the transfected construct (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Analysis of live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Expression of H3 T118E:YFP or H3 T118I:YFP results in lagging chromosomes that delay cytokinesis.
source: From these experiments, we conclude that expression of H3 T118I and T118E results in lagging chromosomes that delay cytokinesis.
evidence: Integration of observations from Figures 3C-E.

claim: An increase in lagging chromosomes is symptomatic of defects in chromosome congression.
source: An increase in lagging chromosomes is symptomatic of defects in chromosome congression (Thompson and Compton, 2011).
evidence: Citation to published work on lagging chromosomes.

claim: Expression of either H3 T118E or T118I significantly decreases the ability to align chromosomes compared to wild type H3 or T118A.
source: Expression of either H3 T118E or T118I significantly decreased the ability to align chromosomes compared to wild type H3 or T118A (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Error correction assay data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: An over abundance of H3 T118E and T118I mutants may hinder chromosome congression.
source: This result suggests that an over abundance of H3 T118E and T118I mutants may hinder chromosome congression.
evidence: Inference from error correction assay results.

claim: Control animals bearing wild type H3 survived to adulthood in Drosophila.
source: While control animals bearing wild type H3 survived to adulthood, animals expressing the mutant H3 T118A, E and I died as embryos after depletion of the maternal contribution of histones (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Drosophila viability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Animals expressing the mutant H3 T118A, E and I died as embryos after depletion of the maternal contribution of histones in Drosophila.
source: While control animals bearing wild type H3 survived to adulthood, animals expressing the mutant H3 T118A, E and I died as embryos after depletion of the maternal contribution of histones (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Drosophila viability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Normal levels of H3 T118ph are essential for development.
source: These results indicate that normal levels of H3 T118ph are essential for development.
evidence: Inference from Drosophila lethality data.

claim: H3 T118ph remains at centromeres of misaligned chromosomes along with the spindle assembly checkpoint kinase BubRI, even in metaphase.
source: Caffeine was used to induce misaligned chromosomes (Katsuki et al., 2008). H3 T118ph remained at centromeres of misaligned chromosome along with the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) kinase BubRI, even in metaphase (Figure 4A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data with caffeine treatment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Removal of H3 T118ph is triggered by chromosome alignment.
source: This suggests that removal of H3 T118ph is triggered by chromosome alignment and led us to speculate that H3 T118ph plays a role in achieving efficient chromosome attachment.
evidence: Inference from observation that H3 T118ph remains on misaligned chromosomes.

claim: Outer-kinetochore proteins, spindle assembly checkpoint proteins and the heterochromatin landscape are indistinguishable between cells expressing H3 T118A, T118E, T118I or wild type H3.
source: Accordingly, we investigated the potential molecular reasons for the defect in chromosome congression caused by H3 T118E and T118I. Outer-kinetochore proteins, spindle assembly checkpoint proteins and the heterochromatin landscape were indistinguishable between cells expressing H3 T118A, T118E, T118I or wild type H3 (data not shown).
evidence: Statement of experimental observations.

claim: Misaligned chromosomes in H3 T118I and T118E mutants are capable of forming proper kinetochores and recruiting SAC proteins.
source: Taken together, these data show that misaligned chromosomes in H3 T118I and T118E mutants are capable of forming proper kinetochores and recruiting SAC proteins
evidence: Integration of observations about kinetochore and SAC proteins.

claim: Mitotic spreads from cells expressing wild type H3 or H3 T118A upon pro-metaphase arrest and metaphase arrest mostly have closely associated sister chromatids with 'closed' or 'open' arms.
source: Mitotic spreads from cells expressing wild type H3 or H3 T118A upon pro-metaphase arrest (induced by Monastrol) and metaphase arrest (Monastrol arrest released into MG132) mostly had closely associated sister chromatids with 'closed' or 'open' arms (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Mitotic spread analysis shown in Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3 T118E or T118I causes a higher incidence of chromosomes with 'partially separated' arms, indicating loss of arm cohesion and partial loss of centromeric cohesion.
source: By contrast, H3 T118E or H3 T118I caused a higher incidence of chromosomes with "partially separated" arms, indicating loss of arm cohesion and partial loss of centromeric cohesion (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Mitotic spread analysis shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The loss of cohesion is most pronounced for H3 T118I, where partially separated sister chromatids are predominant in 50% of the cells versus 10% of the cells for wild type H3.
source: The loss of cohesion was most pronounced for H3 T118I, where partially separated sister chromatids were predominant in 50% of the cells versus 10% of the cells for wild type H3 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantitation of cohesion defects shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The proportion of cells where most of the sister chromatids are totally separated is 16% for H3 T118I versus 4% for wild type H3.
source: Furthermore, the proportion of cells where most of the sister chromatids were totally separated, indicating complete loss of cohesion, was 16% for H3 T118I versus 4% for wild type H3 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantitation of cohesion defects shown in Figure 4C.

claim: H3 T118E or H3 T118I promotes loss of cohesion at the centromere and chromosome arms.
source: These data indicate that H3 T118E or H3 T118I promotes loss of cohesion at the centromere and chromosome arms.
evidence: Integration of cohesion defect observations from Figure 4B,C.

claim: The faulty cohesion caused by expression of H3 T118I or T118E is responsible for the defects in chromosome alignment.
source: Given the correlation between faulty cohesion and chromosome alignment defects, we propose that the faulty cohesion caused by expression of H3 T118I or T118E is responsible for the defects in chromosome alignment.
evidence: Inference from correlation between cohesion and alignment defects.

claim: Aurora-A overexpression has been linked to aneuploidy and cancer, presumably through its role in centrosome duplication.
source: Aurora-A overexpression has been linked to aneuploidy and cancer, presumably through its role in centrosome duplication.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Overexpression of Aurora-A increases levels of H3 T118ph along the chromosome arms.
source: Overexpression of Aurora-A increased levels of H3 T118ph along the chromosome arms (Figure 4D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data on chromosome spreads shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upon colcemid-induced pro-metaphase arrest, overexpression of Aurora-A causes 44% of the sister chromatids to be 'partially separated' as compared to 20% for the control cell line.
source: Upon colcemid-induced pro-metaphase arrest, overexpression of Aurora-A caused 44% of the sister chromatids to be "partially separated" as compared to 20% for the control cell line (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Quantitation of cohesion defects shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Overexpression of Aurora-A leads to cohesion loss.
source: Because overexpression of Aurora-A leads to cohesion loss, it is likely that cohesion loss in the H3 T118E and T118I mutants is due to their structurally mimicking elevated levels of H3 T118ph.
evidence: Integration of Aurora-A overexpression and H3 mutant data.

claim: Expression of H3 T118E and T118I makes chromosome one significantly wider and shorter.
source: Expression of H3 T118E and T118I made chromosome one significantly wider and shorter (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Chromosome measurement data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: H3 T118E and T118I significantly increase sister chromatid interkinetochore distances.
source: We found that H3 T118E and T118I significantly increased sister chromatid interkinetochore distances (Figure 5B), as measured by immunostaining for CENP-A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Interkinetochore distance measurements shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Upon pro-metaphase arrest, chromosomes from the H3 wild type and T118A mutant cell lines are organized into loops and coils to form very tight compact structures.
source: Upon pro-metaphase arrest, chromosomes from the H3 wild type and T118A mutant cell lines were organized into loops and coils to form very tight compact structures (Figure 5C).
evidence: SEM imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes from the H3 T118E and T118I cell lines are less tightly packed with longer radiating DNA loops.
source: By contrast, mitotic chromosomes from the H3 T118E and T118I cell lines were less tightly packed with longer radiating DNA loops.
evidence: SEM imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: H3 T118E and T118I disrupt the higher order chromatin packaging.
source: These results indicate that H3 T118E and T118I disrupt the higher order chromatin packaging.
evidence: Inference from SEM and chromosome measurement data.

claim: H3 T118I is more readily extracted from chromatin than wild type H3 at 600 mM salt.
source: In agreement, H3 T118I was more readily extracted from chromatin than wild type H3 at 600 mM salt (Figure 5D).
evidence: Salt extraction assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of H3 T118I increases DNA accessibility to the nuclease DNase I in both asynchronous and mitotically arrested cells.
source: Expression of H3 T118I also increased DNA accessibility to the nuclease DNase I in both asynchronous and mitotically arrested cells (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: DNase I digestion assay data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: These results are consistent with biochemical studies that showed that mononucleosomes with H3 T118ph favor the removal of histone H3 from DNA compared to unphosphorylated mononucleosomes.
source: Together, these results are consistent with biochemical studies that showed that mononucleosomes with H3 T118ph favor the removal of histone H3 from DNA compared to unphosphorylated mononucleosomes (North et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to published biochemical studies and consistency with current observations.

claim: Overexpression of Aurora-A causes significant widening and shortening of the chromosome arms of metaphase chromosomes.
source: Overexpression of Aurora-A caused significant widening and shortening of the chromosome arms of metaphase chromosomes (Figure 5F) as was observed for H3 T118E and T118I (Figure 5A), while overexpression of Aurora-A KD did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Chromosome measurement data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Overexpression of Aurora-A causes increased sister chromatid interkinetochore distances.
source: Overexpression of Aurora-A also caused increased sister chromatid interkinetochore distances (Figure 5G).
evidence: Interkinetochore distance measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The H3 T118I and T118E mutations are functional mimics of H3 T118 phosphorylation in vivo.
source: These results further indicate that the H3 T118I and T118E mutations are functional mimics of H3 T118 phosphorylation in vivo, and show that H3 T118ph disrupts higher order chromatin packaging.
evidence: Integration of observations from H3 mutants and Aurora-A overexpression.

claim: H3 T118ph disrupts higher order chromatin packaging.
source: These results further indicate that the H3 T118I and T118E mutations are functional mimics of H3 T118 phosphorylation in vivo, and show that H3 T118ph disrupts higher order chromatin packaging.
evidence: Integration of multiple lines of evidence from chromosome structure analyses.

claim: During mitotic delay, the intensity of the Rad21/Scc1 component of the cohesion complex along chromosome arms and at centromeres is drastically reduced in cells expressing H3 T118E and T118I.
source: During mitotic delay, the intensity of the Rad21/Scc1 component of the cohesion complex along chromosome arms and at centromeres was drastically reduced in cells expressing H3 T118E and T118I (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data on mitotic spreads shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The T118I and T118E mutants still display cohesion loss despite inhibition of separase with MG132.
source: The fact that the T118I and T118E mutants still displayed cohesion loss, despite inhibition of separase (Figure 6B), indicates that cohesin loss in the T118E/I mutants is not due to premature separase activity.
evidence: Cohesion analysis with MG132 treatment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cohesin loss in the T118E/I mutants is not due to premature separase activity.
source: The fact that the T118I and T118E mutants still displayed cohesion loss, despite inhibition of separase (Figure 6B), indicates that cohesin loss in the T118E/I mutants is not due to premature separase activity.
evidence: Inference from MG132 experiment results.

claim: The PLK-1 inhibitor BI2536 and the Aurora-B inhibitor hesperidin prevent cohesion loss in all the H3 expressing cell lines.
source: We found that the PLK-1 inhibitor, BI2536, and the Aurora-B inhibitor, hesperidin, prevented cohesion loss in all the H3 expressing cell lines (Figure 6B).
evidence: Cohesion analysis with kinase inhibitors shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Topo II inhibitor ICRF-193 causes chromosomes to become extremely tangled, indicating that DNA catenation is undisturbed by the H3 T118 mutations.
source: To prevent DNA decatenation, we used a specific inhibitor of Topo II, ICRF-193 and found that chromosomes became extremely tangled, indicative that DNA catenation is undisturbed by the H3 T118 mutations (Figure 6B).
evidence: Cohesion analysis with ICRF-193 shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The H3 T118I and T118E mutations do not disrupt the proper establishment of sister chromatid cohesion by both DNA and sister chromatid catenation, but are likely to lead to premature cohesion loss via the PLK-1 or Aurora-B mediated pathway.
source: Taken, together, these data indicate the H3 T118I and T118E mutations do not disrupt the proper establishment of sister chromatid cohesion by both DNA and sister chromatid catenation, but are likely to lead to premature cohesion loss via the PLK-1 or Aurora-B mediated pathway.
evidence: Integration of results from multiple inhibitor experiments.

claim: Upon PLK-1 inhibition, chromosomes from cells expressing H3 T118I are extremely short.
source: During our PLK-1 inhibition studies, we observed that chromosomes from cells expressing H3 T118I were extremely short (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), a phenotype observed previously (van Vugt et al., 2004).
evidence: Chromosome spread data with PLK-1 inhibition shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Short chromosomes occur in 90% of the mitotic spreads from PLK-1 inhibited cells expressing H3 T118I compared to 22% for wild type H3.
source: These short chromosomes occurred in 90% of the mitotic spreads from PLK-1 inhibited cells expressing H3 T118I compared to 22% for wild type H3.
evidence: Quantitation of short chromosome phenotype shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The hypercondensation phenotype suggests that H3 T118I may disrupt chromosome scaffolding proteins involved in shaping mitotic chromosomes, including condensin I and II and Topo II.
source: This hypercondensation phenotype suggests that H3 T118I may disrupt chromosome scaffolding proteins involved in shaping mitotic chromosomes, including condensin I and II and Topo II.
evidence: Inference from hypercondensation phenotype.

claim: H3 T118ph does not co-localize with Topo II.
source: However, H3 T118ph does not co-localize with Topo II (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) or condensin I (Figure 7B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence co-localization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7B.

claim: H3 T118ph does not co-localize with condensin I.
source: However, H3 T118ph does not co-localize with Topo II (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) or condensin I (Figure 7B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence co-localization data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The staining of Topo II is similar among cells expressing wild type or mutant H3.
source: The staining of Topo II (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) and condensin II (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A,B) was similar among cells expressing wild type or mutant H3.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The staining of condensin II is similar among cells expressing wild type or mutant H3.
source: The staining of Topo II (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) and condensin II (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A,B) was similar among cells expressing wild type or mutant H3.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Upon mitotic delay by the error correction assay, there is a significant loss of turbo-GFP tagged condensin I CAP-H protein in both H3 T118E (25% of mitotic cells are tGFP negative) and T118I (50% of mitotic cells are tGFP negative) cell lines as compared to wild type H3 (0% of mitotic cells are GFP negative).
source: However upon mitotic delay, by the error correction assay, there was a significant loss of turbo-GFP (tGFP) tagged condensin I CAP-H protein in both H3 T118E (25% of mitotic cells were tGFP negative) and T118I (50% of mitotic cells were tGFP negative) cell lines as compared to wild type H3 (0% of mitotic cells were GFP negative) (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Quantitation of condensin I loss shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: H3 T118I and T118E result in reduced levels of condensin I, but not condensin II or Topo II, on chromatin.
source: These data demonstrate that H3 T118I and T118E results in reduced levels of condensin I, but not condensin II or Topo II, on chromatin, suggesting that H3 T118ph plays a role in reducing condensin I occupancy on the chromatin.
evidence: Integration of observations about scaffold proteins.

claim: H3 T118ph plays a role in reducing condensin I occupancy on the chromatin.
source: These data demonstrate that H3 T118I and T118E results in reduced levels of condensin I, but not condensin II or Topo II, on chromatin, suggesting that H3 T118ph plays a role in reducing condensin I occupancy on the chromatin.
evidence: Inference from condensin I loss in H3 mutants.

claim: Condensin I can bind to nucleosomes and the altered histone-DNA forms, irrespective of the phosphorylation status of H3 T118.
source: In electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) at higher levels of condensin 1, we found that condensin I could bind to nucleosomes and the altered histone-DNA forms, irrespective of the phosphorylation status of H3 T118.
evidence: EMSA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: H3 T118ph does not directly affect condensin I binding to a mononucleosome.
source: This result indicates that H3 T118ph does not directly affect condensin I binding to a mononucleosome.
evidence: Inference from EMSA results.

claim: H3 T118ph promotes changes in global chromatin packaging that may indirectly reduce condensin I occupancy.
source: As such, we favor the idea that H3 T118ph promotes changes in global chromatin packaging that may indirectly reduce condensin I occupancy.
evidence: Inference from lack of direct binding effect and observed chromatin changes.

claim: Upon mitotic delay, there is a significant loss of condensin I from chromatin upon Aurora-A overexpression (25% of mitotic cells are GFP negative) as compared to the control (0% of mitotic cells are GFP negative).
source: Indeed, upon mitotic delay, there was a significant loss of condensin I from chromatin upon Aurora-A overexpression (25% of mitotic cells were GFP negative) as compared to the control (0% of mitotic cells were GFP negative) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Quantitation of condensin I loss with Aurora-A overexpression shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Excess H3 T118ph leads to condensin I loss from chromatin.
source: This result shows that excess H3 T118ph leads to condensin I loss from chromatin.
evidence: Integration of Aurora-A overexpression and H3 mutant data.

claim: The function of mitotic H3 T118ph is to indirectly reduce condensin I and cohesin occupancy on chromatin via its influence on chromosome packaging.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the function of mitotic H3 T118ph is to indirectly reduce condensin I and cohesin occupancy on chromatin via its influence on chromosome packaging.
evidence: Integration of all observations about condensin I, cohesin, and chromatin structure.

claim: H3 T118ph is dynamically regulated through mitosis by the Aurora-A kinase, occurring at pericentromeric regions and at discrete locations on chromosome arms.
source: In metazoans, H3 T118ph is dynamically regulated through mitosis by the Aurora-A kinase, occurring at pericentromeric regions and at discrete locations on chromosome arms.
evidence: Summary of localization and kinase identification data.

claim: Excess H3 T118ph (achieved by overexpression of Aurora-A or mimicked by amino acid substitution) results in increased numbers of lagging chromosomes, defects in chromosome congression, delayed cytokinesis, altered chromosome compaction, cohesion loss and cohesin and condensin I loss.
source: Excess H3 T118ph (achieved by overexpression of Aurora-A or mimicked by amino acid substitution) resulted in increased numbers of lagging chromosomes, defects in chromosome congression, delayed cytokinesis, altered chromosome compaction, cohesion loss and cohesin and condensin I loss.
evidence: Summary of phenotypes from H3 mutants and Aurora-A overexpression.

claim: H3 T118ph disappears from each chromosome when chromosome alignment is achieved.
source: Normally, H3 T118ph disappears from each chromosome when chromosome alignment is achieved.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence time course.

claim: Condensin I increases the rigidity at the centromere.
source: Given that condensin I increases the rigidity at the centromere (Ribeiro et al., 2009), we propose a model where H3 T118ph alters the chromatin structure to limit condensin I and cohesin occupancy in order to enable efficient attachment to the mitotic spindle and effective chromosome compaction (Figure 8).
evidence: Citation to published work on condensin I function.

claim: H3 T118ph alters the chromatin structure to limit condensin I and cohesin occupancy in order to enable efficient attachment to the mitotic spindle and effective chromosome compaction.
source: Given that condensin I increases the rigidity at the centromere (Ribeiro et al., 2009), we propose a model where H3 T118ph alters the chromatin structure to limit condensin I and cohesin occupancy in order to enable efficient attachment to the mitotic spindle and effective chromosome compaction (Figure 8).
evidence: Model proposed based on integration of all experimental observations.

claim: Aurora-A is best known for its role in centrosome separation.
source: Aurora-A is best known for its role in centrosome separation (Dutertre et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation to established knowledge about Aurora-A.

claim: Aurora-A is involved in chromosome error correction through its role in phosphorylating H3 T118 on chromatin.
source: Our data further supports Aurora-A's involvement in chromosome error correction (Chmátal et al., 2015; Ye et al., 2015), specifically through its role in phosphorylating H3 T118 on chromatin.
evidence: Integration of current findings with cited work on Aurora-A in error correction.

claim: The H3 protein sequence K-R-V-T-I fits the R/K/N-R-X-S/T-B consensus site for Aurora-A (where B is a hydrophobic residue).
source: In agreement, the H3 protein sequence K-R-V-T-I fits the R/K/N-R-X-S/T-B consensus site for Aurora-A (where B is a hydrophobic residue) (Ferrari et al., 2005).
evidence: Sequence analysis and citation to Aurora-A consensus site.

claim: Aurora-A, in partnership with its activator TPX2, is responsible for phosphorylation of H3 T118 on the chromatin arms and centromeres.
source: We propose that Aurora-A, in partnership with its activator TPX2, is responsible for phosphorylation of H3 T118 on the chromatin arms and centromeres.
evidence: Integration of kinase identification and TPX2 knockdown data.

claim: Aurora-A is detectable at the centromere during mitosis.
source: Fittingly, Aurora-A is detectable at the centromere during mitosis (Chmatal, Yang et al. 2015).
evidence: Citation to published work.

claim: Aurora-A mediates phosphorylation of centromeric proteins including NDC80, CENP-A and CENP-E.
source: Precedent exists for Aurora-A-mediated phosphorylation of centromeric proteins, on substrates including NDC80 (Ye, Deretic et al. 2015), CENP-A (Kunitoku et al., 2003) and CENP-E (Kim et al., 2010a).
evidence: Citations to published work on Aurora-A substrates.

claim: H3 T118 is the first known target for phosphorylation by Aurora-A along chromosome arms.
source: As such, H3 T118 is the first known target for phosphorylation by Aurora-A along chromosome arms.
evidence: Inference from localization data and comparison with known Aurora-A substrates.

claim: The phosphorylation of H3 T118ph will likely require nucleosome disruption by an ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeler given the buried location of this residue within the nucleosome structure.
source: Regardless of how Aurora-A is targeted to chromatin, it is likely that the phosphorylation of H3 T118ph will also require nucleosome disruption by an ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeler given the buried location of this residue within the nucleosome structure.
evidence: Inference from structural position of T118 in the nucleosome.

claim: It is not surprising that the H3 T118A loss of function mutant gave no detectable phenotype in the presence of endogenous H3 T118ph, given that the mutant is only expressed at approximately 10% of the total histone H3 in human cells.
source: Given that we can only express the H3 mutants to be approximately 10% of the total histone H3 in human cells, it is not surprising that the H3 T118A loss of function mutant gave no detectable phenotype in the presence of endogenous H3 T118ph.
evidence: Inference from expression level data.

claim: The H3 T118E and T118I mutants have dominant effects on wild type histones in human cells.
source: In contrast, the H3 T118E and T118I mutants clearly had dominant effects on wild type histones in human cells.
evidence: Summary of phenotypic data from H3 mutants.

claim: Drosophila cell clones expressing only H3 T118A, H3 T118E, or H3 T118I have significant defects in cell growth.
source: It should be noted that Drosophila cell clones expressing only H3 T118A, H3 T118E, or H3 T118I have significant defects in cell growth (Graves et al., submitted).
evidence: Citation to unpublished work.

claim: H3 T118ph acts to physically distort the nucleosomal DNA at the nucleosome dyad in order to loosen the nucleosome structure and generate altered nucleosomal states.
source: H3 T118ph acts to physically distort the nucleosomal DNA at the nucleosome dyad in order to loosen the nucleosome structure and generate altered nucleosomal states (North et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to published biochemical work.

claim: The alterations to the nucleosome structure that are induced by H3 T118ph impact higher order levels of chromosome packaging.
source: Our results show that the alterations to the nucleosome structure that are induced by H3 T118ph impact higher order levels of chromosome packaging.
evidence: Integration of biochemical knowledge with chromosome structure observations.

claim: The T118I mutant gives even more drastic phenotypes than T118E because isoleucine has a large bulky side chain that would distort the trajectory of the nucleosomal DNA around the histone octamer to an even greater extent than glutamic acid.
source: This structural role of phosphorylation of H3 T118 can explain why the T118I mutant gave even more drastic phenotypes than T118E in our experiments. Although isoleucine is not the classic phosphomimetic substitution, it does have a large bulky side chain that would distort the trajectory of the nucleosomal DNA around the histone octamer to an even greater extent than the traditional phosphomimetic of glutamic acid.
evidence: Inference from structural properties of amino acids and phenotypic severity.

claim: Isoleucine mimics the rigidity of phosphate group compared to the flexible side chain of glutamic acid.
source: Furthermore, isoleucine mimics the rigidity of phosphate group compared to the flexible side chain of glutamic acid.
evidence: Structural reasoning about amino acid properties.

claim: Overexpression of the T118 kinase Aurora-A leads to identical phenotypes to T118I, providing functional support for the idea that H3 T118I structurally mimics the effect of phosphorylation of T118.
source: Functional support for the idea that H3 T118I structurally mimics the effect of phosphorylation of T118 comes from the fact that overexpression of the T118 kinase, Aurora-A, leads to identical phenotypes to T118I.
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes from Aurora-A overexpression and T118I mutant.

claim: H3 T118ph appears at pericentromeric regions during prophase and disappears from each chromosome as it aligns at the metaphase plate.
source: H3 T118ph appears at pericentromeric regions during prophase and disappears from each chromosome as it aligns at the metaphase plate.
evidence: Summary of temporal localization data.

claim: H3 T118ph plays an important role in organizing the chromatin structure around centromeres to achieve optimal levels of cohesin and condensin I association to permit enough conformational flexibility for microtubule attachment.
source: Accordingly, we propose that H3 T118ph plays an important role in organizing the chromatin structure around centromeres to achieve optimal levels of cohesin and condensin I association to permit enough conformational flexibility for microtubule attachment.
evidence: Model proposed based on integration of observations about H3 T118ph, condensin I, cohesin, and chromosome alignment.

claim: Condensin I is highly enriched at centromeres in mitosis in metazoans.
source: Condensin I is highly enriched at centromeres in mitosis in metazoans (Kim et al., 2013) and promotes the rigidity of the centromere (Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: Citations to published work on condensin I localization and function.

claim: Condensin I promotes the rigidity of the centromere.
source: Condensin I is highly enriched at centromeres in mitosis in metazoans (Kim et al., 2013) and promotes the rigidity of the centromere (Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to published work.

claim: Aurora-A has been demonstrated to play a role in error correction by destabilizing microtubule connections of misaligned chromosomes.
source: Additionally, Aurora–A has been demonstrated to play a role in error correction by destabilizing microtubule connections of misaligned chromosomes. Upon knockdown or inhibition of Aurora-A the kinetochore, as well as their attachment to microtubules, become more rigid and stable (Chmatal, Yang et al. 2015, Ye, Deretic et al. 2015).
evidence: Citations to published work on Aurora-A in error correction.

claim: Upon knockdown or inhibition of Aurora-A, the kinetochore and their attachment to microtubules become more rigid and stable.
source: Upon knockdown or inhibition of Aurora-A the kinetochore, as well as their attachment to microtubules, become more rigid and stable (Chmatal, Yang et al. 2015, Ye, Deretic et al. 2015).
evidence: Citations to published work.

claim: H3 T118ph at the centromere acts to limit condensin I occupancy in order to increase flexibility at the centromeres of misaligned chromosomes.
source: As such, H3 T118ph at the centromere appears to act to limit condensin I occupancy in order to increase flexibility at the centromeres of misaligned chromosomes (Figure 8).
evidence: Model proposed based on integration of observations about H3 T118ph, condensin I, and chromosome alignment.

claim: Chromosomes from cells expressing H3 T118E, T118I or overexpressing Aurora-A have increased interkinetochore distances, which could be indirectly or directly related to the role of H3 T118ph in removal of cohesin and condensin I.
source: This idea is supported by chromosomes from cells expressing H3 T118E, T118I or overexpressing Aurora-A having increased interkinetochore distances (Figure 5B,G), which could be indirectly or directly related to the role of H3 T118ph in removal of cohesin and condensin I.
evidence: Interkinetochore distance data and inference about mechanism.

claim: Upon attachment to mitotic spindles from opposite centrosomes, the centromeric regions have to be rigid enough to resist the forces that the microtubules exert on the centromere in order to prevent separation of sister chromatids until anaphase.
source: However, upon attachment to mitotic spindles from opposite centrosomes, the centromeric regions have to be rigid enough to resist the forces that the microtubules exert on the centromere in order to prevent separation of sister chromatids until anaphase (Musacchio and Salmon, 2007).
evidence: Citation to published work on centromere mechanics.

claim: Removal of H3 T118ph as soon as tension is sensed across the kinetochores would allow for better centromere rigidity.
source: Removal of H3 T118ph as soon as tension is sensed across the kinetochores would allow for better centromere rigidity.
evidence: Model proposed based on timing of H3 T118ph loss and centromere mechanics.

claim: H3 T118ph plays a role in achieving appropriate microtubule attachment, consistent with H3 T118ph remaining at centromeres of misaligned chromosomes.
source: Consistent with an important role for H3 T118ph in achieving appropriate microtubule attachment, H3 T118ph remained at centromeres of misaligned chromosomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observation from caffeine-induced misalignment experiment.

claim: H3 T118ph occurs in a punctate periodic pattern along chromosome arms in prophase and pro-metaphase.
source: H3 T118ph occurs in a punctate periodic pattern along chromosome arms in prophase and pro-metaphase.
evidence: Summary of localization data on chromosome arms.

claim: Excess H3 T118ph leads to gross alterations in chromosome compaction, with wider and shorter chromosome arms and longer, less organized chromatin loops, suggesting that H3 T118ph plays a role in shaping mitotic chromosomes.
source: Excess H3 T118ph (due to overexpression of Aurora-A or mutations that mimic the effect of phosphorylation) leads to gross alterations in chromosome compaction, with wider and shorter chromosome arms and longer, less organized chromatin loops (Figure 5), suggesting that H3 T118ph plays a role in shaping mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: Summary of chromosome structure data and inference about function.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes are packaged in a two phase process: in the first phase, a linear array of chromatin loops form at random, but consistent, positions along the chromosome; in the second phase, the loops longitudinally condense around the axes.
source: Mitotic chromosomes have been suggested to be packaged in a two phase process (Naumova et al., 2013). In the first phase, a linear array of chromatin loops form at random, but consistent, positions along the chromosome. In the second phase, the loops longitudinally condense around the axes.
evidence: Citation to published model of chromosome packaging.

claim: Condensin II is required for linear compaction along the chromosome axes while condensin I helps organize chromatin loops around the axes.
source: These two different phases are mediated by the condensins, where condensin II is required for linear compaction along the chromosome axes while condensin I helps organize chromatin loops around the axes (Shintomi and Hirano, 2010, Green et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to published work on condensin functions.

claim: The timing of appearance of H3 T118ph and condensin I on chromosome arms is similar, but their spatial localization along the arms is distinct.
source: Although the timing of appearance of H3 T118ph and condensin I on chromosome arms is similar, their spatial localization along the arms are distinct (Figure 7B).
evidence: Comparison of localization patterns from immunofluorescence data.

claim: There is no evidence that H3 T118ph physically recruits or displaces condensin I from chromatin.
source: As such, there is no evidence that H3 T118ph physically recruits or displaces condensin I from chromatin.
evidence: Inference from distinct localization patterns and EMSA results.

claim: Proteins that promote condensin recruitment in yeast include kinetochore proteins and the Ku heterodimer complex, which functions in non-homologous end joining.
source: Indeed, other proteins promote condensin recruitment in yeast including kinetochore proteins (Tada et al., 2011) and the Ku heterodimer complex, which functions in non-homologous end joining (Tanaka et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to published work on condensin recruitment.

claim: Yeast condensin interacts with histone H2A and H2AZ in vitro.
source: Perhaps related to its recruitment mechanism, yeast condensin interacts with histone H2A and H2AZ in vitro (Tada et al., 2011) and cross-linking mass spectrometry studies have found interactions between condensin I and H2A and H4 (Barysz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations to published work on condensin-histone interactions.

claim: Cross-linking mass spectrometry studies have found interactions between condensin I and H2A and H4.
source: Perhaps related to its recruitment mechanism, yeast condensin interacts with histone H2A and H2AZ in vitro (Tada et al., 2011) and cross-linking mass spectrometry studies have found interactions between condensin I and H2A and H4 (Barysz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to published work.

claim: H3 T118 phosphorylation is likely to regulate condensin I occupancy on the chromatin, given that expression of H3 T118I, T118E and overexpression of Aurora-A cause loss of condensin I from chromosome arms.
source: In addition, our evidence indicates that H3 T118 phosphorylation is likely to regulate condensin I occupancy on the chromatin, given that expression of H3 T118I, T118E and overexpression of Aurora-A cause loss of condensin I from chromosome arms (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Integration of condensin I loss data from H3 mutants and Aurora-A overexpression.

claim: The disruption of condensin I function is in agreement with the longer loops of chromatin that were observed by SEM in the T118E and T118I mutants.
source: This disruption of condensin I function is in agreement with the longer loops of chromatin that were observed by SEM in the T118E and T118I mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: Correlation between condensin I loss and chromatin loop phenotype.

claim: The H3 T118I and T118E mutants cause a delay in cytokinesis, consistent with the delayed cytokinesis that occurs upon condensin I knockdown.
source: Consistent with the delayed cytokinesis that occurs upon condensin I knockdown (Gerlich et al., 2006) the H3 T118I and T118E mutants caused a delay in cytokinesis (Figure 3E).
evidence: Comparison of cytokinesis phenotype with published condensin I knockdown phenotype.

claim: Condensin I interacts with chromosomes in a more dynamic manner than condensin II.
source: Given that condensin I interacts with chromosomes in a more dynamic manner than condensin II (Gerlich et al., 2006),we propose that the dynamic nature of the association of condensin I with chromatin enables H3 T118ph to regulate the levels of condensin I to shape the mitotic chromosomes as they condense.
evidence: Citation to published work on condensin dynamics.

claim: The dynamic nature of the association of condensin I with chromatin enables H3 T118ph to regulate the levels of condensin I to shape the mitotic chromosomes as they condense.
source: Given that condensin I interacts with chromosomes in a more dynamic manner than condensin II (Gerlich et al., 2006),we propose that the dynamic nature of the association of condensin I with chromatin enables H3 T118ph to regulate the levels of condensin I to shape the mitotic chromosomes as they condense.
evidence: Model proposed based on condensin dynamics and H3 T118ph effects.

claim: The ratio of condensin I to condensin II is very tightly controlled within cells, and changes in the ratio profoundly alter the shape of mitotic chromosomes.
source: The ratio of condensin I to condensin II is very tightly controlled within cells, given that changes in the ratio profoundly alters the shape of mitotic chromosomes (Shintomi and Hirano, 2010, Bakhrebah et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations to published work on condensin ratios.

claim: The removal of H3 T118ph from the chromosome arms by metaphase is likely to regulate the ratio of condensin I:condensin II for appropriate chromosome compaction.
source: As such, the removal of H3 T118ph from the chromosome arms by metaphase, either by dephosphorylation or by our preferred model of physical removal of T118 phosphorylated H3 from the DNA, is likely to regulate the ratio of condensin I:condensin II for appropriate chromosome compaction.
evidence: Model proposed based on timing of H3 T118ph loss and condensin ratio importance.

claim: The removal of H3 T118ph from chromosome arms likely occurs via physical removal of T118 phosphorylated H3 from the DNA rather than dephosphorylation.
source: As such, the removal of H3 T118ph from the chromosome arms by metaphase, either by dephosphorylation or by our preferred model of physical removal of T118 phosphorylated H3 from the DNA, is likely to regulate the ratio of condensin I:condensin II for appropriate chromosome compaction.
evidence: Preferred model stated by authors.

claim: The loss of condensin I function occurs in an indirect manner via H3 T118ph affecting chromatin structure, given that condensin I binding to mononucleosomes is not affected by H3 T118ph in vitro.
source: This function is likely to occur in an indirect manner via H3 T118ph affecting chromatin structure, given that condensin I binding to mononucleosomes is not affected by H3 T118ph in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Inference from EMSA results showing no direct binding effect.

claim: The loss of cohesin is an indirect consequence of the altered packaging of the chromatin structure caused by excess H3 T118ph, which may expose the cohesin ring to PLK-1 mediated phosphorylation and subsequent removal of cohesin.
source: Similarly, we propose that the loss of cohesin is an indirect consequence of the altered packaging of the chromatin structure caused by excess H3 T118ph, which may expose the cohesin ring to PLK-1 mediated phosphorylation and subsequent removal of cohesin (Hauf et al., 2005).
evidence: Model proposed based on chromatin structure changes and PLK-1 inhibitor results.

claim: The cohesion phenotype may be due to loss of Sgo-1-mediated protection against PLK-1 and Aurora-B kinases.
source: However, we were unable to rule out the possibility that the cohesion phenotype may be due to loss of Sgo-1-mediated protection against PLK-1 and Aurora-B kinases.
evidence: Statement of alternative mechanism that could not be ruled out.

claim: Phosphorylation of H3 T118 at the nucleosome dyad by Aurora-A is a critical step to ensure chromosome congression, via its influence on chromosome compaction and cohesion through physically regulating nucleosome structure.
source: Taken together, our work suggests a model where phosphorylation of H3 T118 at the nucleosome dyad by Aurora-A is a critical step to ensure chromosome congression, via its influence on chromosome compaction and cohesion through physically regulating nucleosome structure.
evidence: Summary model integrating all observations.

claim: The functions of H3 T118ph are likely to be conserved in metazoans, as similar localization and timing of H3 T118ph is found in nematodes, flies, and human cells.
source: These functions are likely to be conserved in metazoans, as we find similar localization and timing of H3 T118ph in nematodes, flies, and human cells.
evidence: Summary of conservation data across species.

claim: The importance of the ability to utilize H3 T118ph to alter the nucleosome structure to regulate mitosis is underscored by the embryonic lethality of flies where all of their histones are mutated to prevent T118 phosphorylation or to mimic persistent H3 T118 phosphorylation.
source: The importance of the ability to utilize H3 T118ph to alter the nucleosome structure to regulate mitosis is underscored by the embryonic lethality of flies where all of their histones are mutated to prevent T118 phosphorylation or to mimic persistent H3 T118 phosphorylation.
evidence: Integration of Drosophila lethality data with functional model.

claim: The carcinogenic effect of overexpressed Aurora-A may be mediated at least in part via altering the mitotic chromatin structure by phosphorylation at the nucleosome dyad.
source: Given that Aurora-A is overexpressed in many cancers, it is tempting to speculate that the carcinogenic effect of overexpressed Aurora-A may be mediated at least in part via altering the mitotic chromatin structure by phosphorylation at the nucleosome dyad.
evidence: Speculation based on Aurora-A overexpression in cancer and H3 T118ph effects.
